paragraphs: I've worked this end of Moraga long enough to know that a home on Brookfield Drive at the cul-de-sac end of Camino Woods doesn't come along often, and when it does, it tends to get attention. The Viking and Miele kitchen alone signals a level of investment that a lot of buyers in this range are actively looking for. When I saw the listing come off market after just 28 days without a sale, I wanted to reach out, because I don't think the outcome reflects what the home actually offers.

Twenty-eight days is a short run, but the listing history still tells a story. The description leads with 'Stop the search' and leans hard on adjectives, but it doesn't show the buyer what is actually different about this home. A fully renovated kitchen with professional-grade appliances, a cul-de-sac setting, a spa primary suite, and new windows throughout are real, defensible premiums. Buyers at $1,795,000 are comparing carefully, and without a clear visual narrative and a direct case for the price, qualified buyers often move on before they schedule a showing. The home wasn't the problem. The story being told about it was.

I've put together a short packet that looks at where the listing ran into friction and what a different approach would look like for this property specifically. It covers the pricing context, where the marketing left value on the table, and how I'd position the cul-de-sac setting and the kitchen remodel to the buyers who will actually pay for them.

If you're already working with an agent toward a new listing, please feel free to set this aside, no hard feelings at all. If you're still weighing your options and want to talk through what a relaunch could look like, I'd welcome the conversation.

exec_summary.headline: A Fully Renovated Cul-de-Sac Home with Professional-Grade Finishes  -  and a Listing That Undersold Both
exec_summary.p1: 102 Brookfield Drive has the profile Lamorinda buyers at this price point are searching for: a deeply renovated single-story on a quiet cul-de-sac in Camino Woods, with a professional Viking and Miele kitchen, a spa-style primary suite, updated bathrooms, new LED lighting throughout, and all-new replacement windows. These are not cosmetic touches. They are the kind of deliberate, high-cost upgrades that move a 1964 ranch into a different tier of the Moraga market.
exec_summary.p2: The listing ran 28 days and came off market without a sale. At $761 per square foot, the home sits in the premium range of the Moraga benchmark, which is appropriate given the level of renovation. But a price at the upper end of the range requires a marketing case that is equally specific. The listing description relied on superlatives rather than substance, and the visual and narrative story never built the argument that would give a $1,795,000 buyer confidence before they walked in the door. The gap wasn't in the home. It was in what the listing communicated about the home.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch needs to do one thing well: show the right buyer, before they request a showing, exactly why this home is worth $761 per square foot when comparable Moraga homes are not. That case is built on the kitchen, the setting, the renovation depth, and the cul-de-sac privacy, told visually and specifically, and distributed to buyers who are actively shopping this price range in Lamorinda.

forensics.title: Friction #1: The Premium Was Priced In, But Never Proven
forensics.body: At $761 per square foot, 102 Brookfield is sitting at the top of the Moraga premium tier, which runs $750 to $820. That number is defensible given the Viking and Miele kitchen, the spa primary suite, the new windows, and the cul-de-sac position. But buyers comparing options at this price point need to understand specifically what they are getting here that they cannot get in a $700 per square foot alternative down the street. The listing led with adjectives like 'beautifully reimagined' and 'stunning' without translating the investment into buyer-facing value. When the premium is asserted but not demonstrated, price-conscious buyers hesitate, and 28 days later the listing is gone.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork uses Zillow Showcase placement to give this home an enhanced listing presence with custom narrative space, so the case for $761 per square foot is made at the first touchpoint, before a buyer ever clicks through to schedule a showing.

forensics.title: Friction #2: The Narrative Read Like a Template, Not a Home
forensics.body: The listing description opened with 'Stop the search, this is the one you've been waiting for' and moved quickly into section headers and fragmented bullet phrases. For buyers shopping at $1,795,000, that register signals a generic listing, not a considered one. The Viking and Miele appliances, the cul-de-sac setting at the quieter end of Brookfield, the spa primary bath, the new LED lighting, the replacement windows, these are specific and credible details that belong in full sentences that show a buyer why this home is different. A listing description that reads like a form template asks buyers to do the work of imagining value rather than feeling it. Buyers who have to work that hard usually don't call.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork writes listing remarks the way a great buyer's agent would describe a home to a motivated client, specific, grounded, and honest about what makes this property worth the drive from the city.

forensics.title: Friction #3: The Visual Story of This Home Was Never Told
forensics.body: A fully renovated kitchen with professional-grade Viking and Miele appliances, a spa-style primary suite, and a cul-de-sac lot with noted privacy and curb appeal are assets that live or die on photography and visual context. Standard MLS photography captures four walls and a countertop. It rarely captures what it feels like to stand in that kitchen, or why the end-of-cul-de-sac setting on Brookfield is meaningfully different from a mid-block address. Buyers searching online at $1.7 million are narrowing their list before they leave the house, and a home that doesn't visually pull them in rarely gets the showing that would close the deal.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Sky Tour gives buyers the aerial context to understand the lot position, the cul-de-sac setting, and the neighborhood character in a way no ground photo can, and a Matterport 3D tour lets out-of-area buyers walk the renovated interior before they ever schedule a trip to Moraga.

positioning_table.verdict: At $761/sqft versus a benchmark range of $750-$820/sqft, this home sits near the lower end of that range. At $761 per square foot, 102 Brookfield sits at the low end of Moraga's premium tier, which means the renovation investment is priced into the home without reaching the ceiling of what the market will bear for the best examples in this category. That is a reasonable and defensible position, but it requires the listing to clearly demonstrate why this home belongs in the premium tier rather than simply asserting it. The strategy going forward needs to close that gap between what the home offers and what the marketing has shown.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Build the Visual Case Before the First Showing
pillars.body: The Viking and Miele kitchen and the spa primary suite are the two assets most likely to pull a qualified buyer off the fence at this price point. But they need to be seen to be believed, and most online buyers are making their shortlist before they leave their couch. BrightWork's Matterport 3D tour lets a buyer in San Francisco walk every room of this home on a Tuesday night, so that by the time they call, they are not curious, they are committed. We lead with visuals because that is where decisions are actually made.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Tell the Cul-de-Sac Story From the Air
pillars.body: The end-of-cul-de-sac position on Brookfield is a genuine differentiator, but it is invisible in a standard street-level photo. A Sky Tour gives buyers the aerial perspective to see the lot position, the privacy buffer, the setting within Camino Woods, and the character of the neighborhood in a way no ground shot can replicate. Buyers paying $1.7 million want to understand what they are buying before they drive out, and a lot's position within its block is one of the things they are paying for.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Reach the Buyers Who Are Ready Before They Find Something Else
pillars.body: The buyer for 102 Brookfield is likely a professional household relocating from San Francisco or Oakland, shopping Moraga and Lafayette simultaneously, and comparing carefully. BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns put this home in front of that buyer pool while they are still in research mode, before they have committed to another property and before they have even fully articulated that Moraga is where they want to land. Passive MLS distribution waits for buyers to find the listing. This approach goes and finds the buyers who are ready.
